Part 1: Tree Fundamentals Binary Trees and Tree Data Structures Why trees exist Arrays, vectors and linked lists all store data in a straight line. That works when the data itself is a line: marks of 50 students, characters of a string, prices over 30 days. A lot of real data is not a line. It is a hierarchy . Company |-- Engineering | |-- Backend | +-- Frontend +-- Sales |-- India +-- Europe Folders inside folders, an HTML page inside body inside html, a tournament bracket, a family lineage, the decision steps of a game. In all of these, one item leads to several items below it, and each of those again leads to more. You cannot express that with a single line of memory without a lot of pain. There is a second reason, a purely practical one. A sorted array searches in O(log N) but inserting in the middle costs O(N). A linked list inserts in O(1) but searches in O(N). A balanced search tree gives you both search and insert in O(log N). Databases, file systems, std::map and std::set are all built on trees for exactly this reason. So trees exist for two reasons: 1. Some data is naturally hierarchical. 2. Some operations are only fast when data is arranged in a branching structure.

For this course we care mostly about the first reason, because that is what LeetCode tree problems test. What is a tree A tree is a set of nodes connected by edges, with three rules: 1. One node is marked special. It is called the root, and it is drawn at the top. 2. Every other node has exactly one node directly above it (its parent). 1

Binary Trees and Tree Data Structures 2 3. There are no cycles. You can never walk down and come back to where you started. Because of rule 2 and 3, a tree with N nodes always has exactly N - 1 edges. Every node except the root consumes exactly one edge to attach itself to its parent. Computer science trees are drawn upside down. Root on top, leaves at the bottom. Get used to it now, every diagram in this material follows that convention. The pair (2, 4) is an edge. Root: the topmost node, node 1. It has no parent. Parent: node 2 is the parent of 4 and 5. Child: 4 and 5 are children of 2. Siblings: nodes with the same parent. 4 and 5 are siblings. 2 and 3 are siblings. Leaf: a node with no children. Here: 4, 5, 6. A leaf is a node where both left and right are NULL. Internal node: any node that is not a leaf. Here: 1, 2, 3. Ancestor: any node on the path from a node up to the root. Ancestors of 5 are 2 and 1. Descendant: everything below a node. A subtree is itself a complete, valid tree. That single fact is what makes recursion work on trees.

Depth of a node: number of edges from the root down to that node. Depth(1) = 0, depth(2) = 1, depth(4) = 2. Depth is measured looking upward, toward the root. Height of a node: number of edges on the longest path from that node down to a leaf. Height(4) = 0, height(2) = 1, height(1) = 2. Height is measured looking downward. Height of the tree: the height of its root. Here, 2. Depth versus height, and the counting trap Depth and height are measured in opposite directions. A leaf has height 0. The root has depth 0. There is a second trap. Some books count edges, some count nodes. A single node alone has height 0 by the edge definition and height 1 by the node definition. Both are used in the real world. LeetCode uses the node count. Problem 104, “Maximum Depth of Binary Tree”, says the depth of the tree above is 3, not 2. Binary tree A binary tree is a tree where every node has at most two children, and the two children are distinguishable: one is the left child, one is the right child. “Distinguishable” is not a detail. These two trees are different trees: 1 1 / \ 2 2 The first has 2 as a left child, the second as a right child. Their inorder traversals differ, their views differ, and a function like “is this tree symmetric” will give different answers. Almost every interview and contest tree problem is about binary trees, which is why we spend the whole course on them. Special shapes of binary trees You need these names to read problem statements. You do not need formal proofs. Full binary tree: every node has either 0 or 2 children. No node has exactly one child.

Binary Trees and Tree Data Structures 4 1 / \ 2 3 / \ 4 5 Complete binary tree: every level is completely filled except possibly the last, and the last level is filled from left to right with no gaps. This is the shape a heap uses, and it is the shape that lets you store a tree in a plain array . 1 / \ 2 3 / \ 4 5 Perfect binary tree: every internal node has 2 children and all leaves are on the same level. 1 / \ 2 3 / \ / \ 4 5 6 7 Skewed or degenerate tree: every node has only one child. It is a linked list wearing a tree costume. 1 \ 2 \ 3 \ 4 Why the shape matters Two numbers you should be able to state instantly: • A perfect tree of height h has 2ˆ(h+1) - 1 nodes. Level d holds at most 2ˆd nodes. • Therefore a balanced tree with N nodes has height about log2(N). For N = 10ˆ6 that is about 20. A skewed tree with N nodes has height N - 1. Every recursive tree algorithm uses O(H) stack space, where H is the height. On a balanced tree that is 20 stack frames. On a skewed tree of 10ˆ5 nodes that is 10ˆ5 stack frames, and on some judges that is a stack overflow. When you see “the tree can be skewed” in constraints, that is the hint. A value, a pointer to the left child, a pointer to the right child. NULL means “there is no child there”. Two observations that carry the whole course: 1. A tree is just a pointer to its root. Why recursion fits trees so naturally A quick recursion refresher A recursive function calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem. It needs two parts: 1. a base case, small enough to answer directly 2. a recursive step, which solves a smaller input and builds the answer from it

Binary Trees and Tree Data Structures 7 int fact(int n) { if (n == 0) return 1; // base case return n * fact(n - 1); // smaller version of the same problem } When you call fact(3), the machine does not magically know the answer. It stacks up pending work: fact(3) waits for fact(2) fact(2) waits for fact(1) fact(1) waits for fact(0) fact(0) = 1 <- base case, now unwind fact(1) = 1 * 1 = 1 fact(2) = 2 * 1 = 2 fact(3) = 3 * 2 = 6 Two things to notice, because they reappear in every tree problem: • The going-down phase and the coming-back-up phase are different moments. You can do work in either one. • Every pending call sits on the call stack, which costs memory . Now the tree version For an array you had to invent the smaller problem: n - 1 , or “the rest of the array”. In a tree the smaller problem is already sitting there. root->left is a smaller tree. root->right is a smaller tree. The structure hands you the recursion for free. So every tree function looks like this: ReturnType solve(TreeNode* root) { if (root == NULL) return answerForEmptyTree; ReturnType L = solve(root->left); // answer for the left subtree ReturnType R = solve(root->right); // answer for the right subtree

The base case is almost always root == NULL . Ask yourself: what is the correct answer for an empty tree? Number of nodes: 0. Height: 0. Sum: 0. Maximum value: negative infinity . Is it balanced: yes. That question, asked honestly , gives you the base case every single time. When a recursive tree solution misbehaves, drawing the call tree for a 5 node example finds the bug faster than any debugger. Common mistakes • Forgetting the NULL base case. Part 2: Depth First Traversals Preorder, Inorder, Postorder What traversal means Traversal means visiting every node exactly once in some fixed order. That is all. An array has one obvious order: left to right. A tree does not. From node 1 you can go to 2 or to 3, and there is no single natural answer. Different orders are useful for different jobs, so we standardise a few of them and give them names. Depth First Search (DFS) means: go as deep as possible down one branch before coming back and trying the other branch. It is what a person does in a maze when they follow one corridor to its end before backtracking. Breadth First Search (BFS) means: finish an entire level before moving to the next. That is Part 3. DFS on a binary tree comes in three flavours. They differ in exactly one thing: when you record the current node relative to the two recursive calls. // preorder visit(node); go(left); go(right); // inorder go(left); visit(node); go(right); // postorder go(left); go(right); visit(node); The names tell you where “root” sits: pre = root first, in = root in the middle, post = root last. In all three, left is always explored before right. The one picture that explains all three

Binary Trees and Tree Data Structures 2 During that walk you touch every node exactly three times: 1. when you arrive at it from above (going down into it) 2. when you come back up from its left subtree 3. when you come back up from its right subtree, just before leaving it for good Now the three traversals are simply three choices of which touch counts: Traversal Record the node on which touch Preorder 1st touch, on the way down Inorder 2nd touch, between left and right Postorder 3rd touch, on the way out The results for our tree: Preorder : 1 2 4 5 3 6 Inorder : 4 2 5 1 3 6 Postorder : 4 5 2 6 3 1 Check those three lines against the picture until they feel obvious. Once this single picture is solid, iterative traversal and Morris traversal later become much less mysterious, because they are just different ways of remembering “which touch am I on”. Preorder traversal Meaning Process the node, then everything on its left, then everything on its right. Root comes before its descendants, always. Binary Trees and Tree Data Structures 3 vector<int> preorderTraversal(TreeNode* root) { vector<int> out; preorder(root, out); return out; } Note the vector<int>&. The ampersand means all calls share one vector. Drop it and every call gets its own copy , the pushes are thrown away , and you return an empty answer. This is one of the most common beginner bugs in tree code. Dry run call preorder(1) record 1 out = [1] call preorder(2) record 2 out = [1,2] call preorder(4) record 4 out = [1,2,4] preorder(NULL) return preorder(NULL) return return from 4 call preorder(5) record 5 out = [1,2,4,5] two NULL calls, return return from 5 return from 2 call preorder(3) record 3 out = [1,2,4,5,3] preorder(NULL) return call preorder(6) record 6 out = [1,2,4,5,3,6] return from 6 return from 3 done out = [1,2,4,5,3,6] As a call tree: pre(1) |-- pre(2) | |-- pre(4) | +-- pre(5) +-- pre(3) +-- pre(6) Read the node values in the order the calls start, and you get the preorder. Complexity Time O(N), space O(H). Same as preorder. When inorder is the right choice • Anything involving a BST. The inorder traversal of a BST is sorted, ascending. This single fact solves a whole family of problems: validate BST (LeetCode 98), kth smallest element (230), minimum absolute difference (530), convert BST to sorted list, and more. • Finding the predecessor or successor of a node in a BST. • Recovering a tree when you are given the inorder array plus preorder or postorder. Why is a BST’s inorder sorted? By definition, everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node and everything in the right subtree is larger. Inorder prints exactly in that order: smaller stuff, node, larger stuff.

On our tree it is 4 2 5 1 3 6, which is nowhere near sorted. That property is a BST property , not a tree property . • In “validate BST”, checking only left->val < root->val < right->val . That is a local check and it is wrong. Either do an inorder walk and confirm it is strictly increasing, or pass a valid (min, max) range downward. • Losing the previous value while validating. You need to remember the previously printed node to compare against, usually a TreeNode* prev kept outside the recursion. Postorder traversal

Binary Trees and Tree Data Structures 6 Meaning Everything on the left, everything on the right, and only then the node itself. The root is always last. Recursive algorithm postorder(node): if node is empty: return postorder(node.left) postorder(node.right) record node C++ void postorder(TreeNode* root, vector<int>& out) { if (root == NULL) return; postorder(root->left, out); postorder(root->right, out); out.push_back(root->val); } Dry run post(1) post(2) post(4) -> record 4 out = [4] post(5) -> record 5 out = [4,5] record 2 out = [4,5,2] post(3) left is NULL post(6) -> record 6 out = [4,5,2,6] record 3 out = [4,5,2,6,3] record 1 out = [4,5,2,6,3,1] Notice the pattern: a node is recorded only after both of its subtrees are completely finished. The root is recorded last, always. Complexity Time O(N), space O(H). When postorder is the right choice This is the most important traversal for problem solving, and students usually underestimate it. Postorder is the traversal for bottom-up information flow.
